books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

stimulus.text:
Free Black men organized to defend their rights. In September 1830, delegates from several Northern states met at Mother Bethel Church in Philadelphia, chose Richard Allen as president, and formed a society to improve the condition of free people of color and plan a settlement in Canada.

At the same time, Northern states were narrowing Black men’s rights: New York’s 1821 constitution dropped the property test for white voters but kept a $250 property requirement for Black voters, and Pennsylvania’s 1838 constitution limited the vote to white men. New York had ended slavery only gradually, with final emancipation in 1827.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the first National Negro Convention, September 1830, from John W. Cromwell, The Early Negro Convention Movement, and of the voting restrictions in the New York constitution of 1821 and the Pennsylvania constitution of 1838.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Cromwell, The Early Negro Convention Movement
stem: Which claim about free Black life in the North is best supported by the passage as a whole?

options.text: Free Black people faced no legal limits anywhere in the North
options.misconception: Voting limits and slow emancipation are both shown.

options.text: Free Black people generally chose to emigrate to Canada
options.misconception: They debated a settlement; most stayed.

options.text: Northern states freed enslaved people at once after independence
options.misconception: New York freed them only gradually, finally in 1827.

options.text: Free Black people built national organizations even as states stripped their rights

rationales.A: Legal limits fill the passage: a $250 voting test in New York, a white-only vote in Pennsylvania, slow emancipation.
rationales.B: The convention planned a settlement, but planning is not moving. Most free Black Northerners stayed where they were.
rationales.C: New York took until 1827 to end slavery, and New Jersey took longer still. Emancipation in the North was gradual.
rationales.D: Delegates built a national society in 1830 while states narrowed the vote. Organizing grew as rights shrank.
rationales.general:
1. Gather both halves of the passage. Conventions and societies on one side; voting limits and slow emancipation on the other.
2. Ask what they add up to. Organization grew while rights shrank.
3. Name the claim. Freedom did not mean equality, and Black leaders answered with organizing.
Background: The 1830 convention met at Mother Bethel, the church Allen had built.
Remember: when a passage shows action and attack together, the claim must hold both.
